I gave THREE stars not FIVE.  I visited here on Sunday, December 22, 2024.  I arrived about 10 minutes before service started and sat in the back right of the audio stand.  I was so excited about worshipping and knew what my heart needed which is why I bypassed my church.  Not to mention I had just moved to the state and I really needed to decompress which is why I sat in the back.

The Praise leader sang a very powerful song and then the other Praise Leader sang, Holy by Cece Winans.  I am standing worshipping and feeling the presence of God while decompressing and ruining my makeup in tears.  Because worship was what I needed.  To no avail, I felt someone touch me and I opened my eyes and this "usher' with salt and pepper hair in locks said to me, "you are going to have to move.  This is where the ushers sit."  I said maam, I am not moving and why are you disturbing me in the middle of worship?  I said, " I am not moving, I was here before service started and there were no reserve seat signs otherwise I would not have sat here."  I continued to worship, and then another mean spirited usher in all black came to me and said the same thing.  Again I asked them, why are you disturbing me during worship?  "Why did you not get to CHURCH before it started to secure your space."  She kept mumbling and I continued to try to worship.  This time, my heart is grieved because these women have no sensitivity at all to the Spirit of the Living God.  As I continue to worship, a third woman with long curly hair and glasses, said to me, "Are your ushering with us today?'  My response was ma'am I am not moving and why did you all not get to church on time and block the seats off?  I said, "I am a visitor and I will not be returning."
This is exactly why I refrain from the African American churches.  They have religion and not relationship with God.  If these women had of been sensitive to the spirit they would have not said anything to me during worship, but could have used Godly wisdom and approached me after service.  They were mean, not sensitive to the spirit and have poor time management otherwise they would have been at church prior to service starting to reserve their seating assignments.  No one knew what I needed except me and God and they ruined it by being more focused on some seats instead of me receiving what I came to get.

Is 'ushering" scriptural?  The position of an usher is not mentioned in the Bible.  However, an usher is a much needed service in today's church.  What that means to me is, since an "usher" is the face of the church there is a certain anointing that each servant must carry if they called to this service, and not being sensitive to the Holy Spirit is not one.  These three women who approached me have no regard or sensitivity to the divine presence of God and we wonder why people don't come out for worship service.  Because of the lack of compassion for others and the lack of knowing how to meet people where they are.

To the Pastor, please reevaluate and train your people.  Please teach them about being sensitive to the Spirit of God, John 4:24.  Please teach them how to manage their time wisely and arrive at church 30 minutes before it starts to block off their section if they don't want visitors sitting in their section.  Pastor, please teach them about having religious behavior.  They are so bent with religiously sitting in the seats where I was sitting that they had no regard to me or the Spirit of the living God that they just had to say something to me because it irritated them so much they could not hold their peace.  They had to do something to disrupt mine instead.  Let's learn better women so we can be better and do better.  Being an usher does not guarantee you a seat in heaven.  So stop worrying about the seats down here on this earth and make sure your behavior and how you live will constitute your seat in heaven.

reviews.text:
This is a place I truly call home. My family and I have been attending and serving at Elevate City Church for over 5 years now, and in that time we’ve experienced the beauty, the challenges, and the incredible growth of a church that started from the ground up.

We’re always excited to share this place with friends, coworkers, and even people we meet for the first time—because Elevate is a place where you can feel loved, welcomed, and safe the moment you walk in.

Our kids absolutely love Elevate Kids and Wake. They look forward to coming every week and serving wherever help is needed. This community has become family to us, and we’re grateful for every moment we get to be part of it

We absolutely love this church, it truly feels like home. As a family of four, we all look forward to Sundays here. If you’re searching for a non-denominational, family-friendly, Jesus-centered church in Sandy Springs, this is the place. And the worship? Simply incredible!

My wife and I went this past Sunday and were shocked by the overwhelming lack of sincerity and respect. Upon walking into the church for the first time, we were not greeted at all. We made our way into the auditorium and sat down. After only 2 songs, the pastor proceeded to spend 20 minutes asking the church for money to help meet their goals. One of the things he mentioned was how, "If you're new to the church, you can donate one of these ways..." Then, emphasized how they needed EVERYONE to donate in order to make THEIR goals a reality.  Meanwhile, my wife and I, who live paycheck to paycheck at the moment, are looking at eachother like, "Is this dude serious!? We barely had the gas to drive here this morning." After that, they immediately began praying over missionaries for Guatemala and then went straight into a Baptism - while neglecting to share what the Biblical significance of Baptism is and why people do it. To top it off, they had several camera guys walking around, 2 of which got very close to our personal space without so much as a smile. It was obvious that the church is more focused with how they look than how they perform. My wife, who hasn't accepted Christ yet was made very uncomfortable by this, and asked to leave. Again, on our way out mid-service, the people who were standing by the front door made no attempts to communicate with us or even acknowledge us. We are new to the area, and will never return to this church after such a negative experience. This church seems to be very money-driven and too concerned with how they look. Lots of production, very little passion. They promote their missionaries in other countries while allowing people in their own city to slip away without a care. If you're new to Christianity or to church, I strongly recommend finding somewhere else to go. Find a church with a higher emphasis on establishing personal connections and building lasting relationships prior to asking for "5 Million dollars."

I have been part of Metropolitan since 1999—nearly a quarter of a century now—and it has truly become my home church, even with the distance from my house. Here, I’ve found genuine warmth, true love, comfort, and liberation.
All three of my children were born and raised in this church, and it has shaped our family in so many ways. Metropolitan isn’t just a place of worship for me; it’s where my heart belongs. “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”

My first experience of this parish left me  a bit disturbed in my spirit. My first impressions: a beautiful church structurally and internally. Gorgeous depictions on the stained glass windows and the architecture was very lovely. Upon walking it, I was disappointed to see that there was no holy water, instead, there was hand sanitizer bottles! My heart dropped. I looked around and saw bags and packages around their baptismal font. It looks like it was really pretty, but all of the stuff hid  it's beauty. Walking to a seat, I genuflected, but I didn't see a lit candle in front, so, I didn't know if our Lord was up there. I looked for our Lord but could not easily find him right away,  as he appeared not to be in the center and front of the church. Instead there was a piano and microphones, and lots of cords. After being there for about 30 mins, I finally saw that he was off to the side near a door. My heart sank even more. Before mass, there was rosary prayer, which I liked alot. While waiting for mass to begin, there was no quiet time, where one can prepare themselves for the sacred mystery. Lots of chatting everywhere, while I saw others trying to pray. A  woman walks up to the lecturn, she greeted everyone, and welcomed those who were present for the first time and then encouraged the congregation to also greet each other. I liked that as well. During the mass, the singing was reflective of the culture that the parish represents, however, the drums seemed to be overkill. It was present in all the singing and responses. It seemed out of place sometimes. After almost all of the singing, people would clap as if watching a performance. I even heard a cowbell a couple of times which also seemed out of place. The homily was solid. I received a nice word from it. The people clapped here also, after the priest was done, as if watching a performance. When the priest held up our Lord, the singers, who were behind him, were standing, instead of kneeling.  While the priest began to administer our Lord, there were a number of people who came from different areas of the church who walked up surrounding the altar.  I don't know if they were deacons, deaconess, or what. They were not in priestly robes. He handed off the blood of our Lord to someone and they passed it around to each other. That seemed so irreverent to me.  Finally, we,  went to receive our Lord. Here, you do not receive him on the tongue, only in the hand. But, you do get to receive his body and blood. I truly appreciated that. And people were just walking out right after receiving our Lord. Like, huh?? The parking lot was horrible. People parked blocking those who were parked in parking spaces. So we and many others were blocked in until the owner of the one car that blocked the entire parking lot came out of the church. That was a nightmare.

Overall, I did not like the experience here. This is the mother church of black Catholic churches? Having him off to the side, no holy water, musical instruments and microphones at the center instead of him, the clapping at the most odd of moments, the drums, all those people up in the altar space, passing his blood around... smh...I was truly sad about all of this. DC is home to many different churches (but that’s probably no surprise if you’re reading this). Having visited quite a few of them, and growing up in the Church, there are three main characteristics that I find to be non-negotiable in a church: (1) a firm, uncompromising commitment to theology rooted in the Bible and the Gospel, (2) a strong emphasis on meaningful worship and abundant opportunities to serve, and (3) a welcoming community where one can genuinely connect with other believers (which is especially important considering DC’s unique, and transient, culture). The District Church (TDC) embodies these qualities. While TDC is a large church, it offers many ways to get connected, including regular newcomers’ meals where visitors can meet the pastors and learn more about TDC’s beliefs, values, mission, and history. It's also worth noting that TDC truly reflects what (I believe) the Church body should look like, that is, people of all races, cultures, and spiritual backgrounds.

I think it's worth checking out, even if you're on the fence.

Metropolitan Community Church was the first church built by the gay community in North America. When the community came together and wanted a church space of its own, there were church properties for sale elsewhere in the District, but none of the owners of those other properties would sell them to the gay community for use as a church. The community instead had to build their own building from the ground up, and that is where the Metropolitan Community Church still is today.

During the peak of the AIDS epidemic, churches elsewhere in the District refused to hold funerals for deceased gay people. It was very difficult to find a place to be buried as a gay person in the District. The Metropolitan Community Church conducted funeral services for all people, regardless of whether the person was a member of its church. It became known as the only church in the District that would have a funeral service for a deceased gay person in the District.

Washington National Cathedral — Where Stone Meets Spirit

Of all the stops on our D.C. trip, the Washington National Cathedral may have been the most breathtaking. Rising from the city like a Gothic prayer carved in stone, it’s hard not to stand in awe beneath those vaulted ceilings and kaleidoscopic stained-glass windows. Sunlight pours through in blues and reds that feel almost alive — as if light itself is worshiping.

For a Marine who’s seen both the best and the worst of humanity, places like this hit differently. The craftsmanship, the patience, the vision it took to build something so enduring — it’s a reminder of what people can create when they’re united by faith and purpose instead of fear and politics.

I sat quietly for a while in the nave, letting the organ notes roll through the arches. It wasn’t about religion so much as reverence — for creation, for sacrifice, for beauty itself.

The cathedral is still under restoration in some areas from the 2011 earthquake, but that somehow adds to its message: even sacred things can crack, and still stand tall.

If you visit, take your time. Look up. Breathe. Remember that every piece of glass and stone was placed by hands that believed in something lasting.

Washington National Cathedral is one of those venues that humbles you the moment you step inside. The scale, the light, the silence between moments… it all slows you down. As a wedding photographer, that’s rare. And powerful.

I’ve photographed a wedding here, and honestly, it’s a dream if you love timeless imagery. The architecture does half the storytelling for you. Long stone aisles, towering columns, soft light filtering through stained glass that changes color as the ceremony unfolds. Every frame feels intentional, even when nothing is staged.

What surprised me - and maybe I’m biased - is how intimate it can feel despite the grandeur. The echoes fade. Emotions don’t. I remember a quiet pause before the vows… you could almost hear everyone breathing. Those are the moments I live for.

From a practical side, the staff is professional and respectful of the couple and vendors. Clear guidelines, but not restrictive. Which matters, a lot, when you’re trying to move quietly and capture real moments without breaking the atmosphere.

If you’re a couple considering the Cathedral and you value meaning, history, and photographs that will still feel relevant in 50 years… this place delivers. No trends. No noise. Just gravity, beauty, and presence.

I’d photograph another wedding there without hesitation.

The Masses are deeply uplifting, offering a sense of renewal and spiritual connection. The reverent yet welcoming atmosphere makes it accessible for both long-time parishioners and first-time visitors. The music and choir elevate the experience, creating a serene environment for prayer or quiet contemplation.

Beyond worship, the basilica is an architectural and artistic treasure. Every corner reveals exquisite artwork, from detailed marble carvings to vibrant mosaics depicting the life of the Virgin Mary. The quiet chapels throughout the basilica provide intimate spaces for reflection, and the outdoor gardens offer a peaceful retreat.

For travelers, history enthusiasts, or anyone seeking a moment of peace in D.C., the basilica is a true gem. It is easy to access, well-maintained, and offers a welcoming experience for people of all backgrounds.

Whether you’re attending a Mass or simply admiring the incredible architecture, a visit here is both inspiring and rejuvenating.

I once saw a photo of the basilica on Instagram and was finally able to visit this beautiful place. All I can say is, "Wow!" Everyone should see this basilica, even if not for our faith, then at least for the architecture! I can't put into words the impression this basilica made on me. My heart rejoices, and I'm grateful that I could worship God in this place! Everyone should simply visit this place! Praise the Lord!

There is a free parking lot across the road to the left of the church. There was no wait or entrance fee. We walked into the bottom floor near the gift shop and first explored the bottom floor. There is a desk near the right hand gift shop with staff to guide you. There are many beautifully decorated chapels, and we stopped by the crypt chapel to pray. Throughout there are some plaques that explain what you are viewing. Upstairs, the main basilica is beautiful beyond words. You can spend hours admiring the tile and artistry work that adorns every inch of the building. The ceiling is so tall. We had to leave before the 12:10 mass and spent about 1 hour there. The gift shop is well stocked with diverse offerings. You can attend at a time where there is a tour but we did not do this.

An absolute must-see in DC! The Basilica is an awe-inspiring sacred space dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary. It is filled with beautiful art and architecture and chapels representing different devotions to  Mary, many of the immigrant communities that comprise the United States, and American saints. Plan to spend at least a couple of hours exploring both the upper church and lower crypt level. The world-class professional choir sings for the 12pm Mass on Sundays and solemnities throughout the year. It’s worth traveling just to hear them!

This church is a comfortable peer with Europe's finest. The solemn grandeur, the American 20th century ness -- the art Deco flourishes and mosaics with objects from the industrial age, the splendor of Catholic design with English (mostly) inscriptions so Vulgate vernacular -- is a heady mix that had me mouthing"I believe". Almost (I'm Jewish.). Hadn't been in a decade and I can honestly say it's a restful restorative place to visit that puts to rest any reflexive 'European is superior's anxieties. America too has men of vision. Notable are ethnicity specific Mary which is a lovely touching very pre-Trump bit of American syncretism.

reviews.text: I am in awe of of clearly God is at work here. How His people are drawing into this body, how the Holy Spirit is so present and moving amongst us! So blessed. Biblical church where God is truly present

To know Union City Church is to live their tagline- "A church united in a world divided." Founded with Biblical principles, it's not conservative or progressive. It's a church that pushes people toward Jesus so that congregants can be bridge builders and a witness to Washington, D.C. That's who Union City is at their core. Now for the details.

1) Service: There are two services- 9:30 a.m. and 11 a.m. every Sunday. Each service starts with 3-4 songs for worship with lyrics projected onto a main screen and two side TVs. Announcements are made by various members of the congregation. Sermons are around 30-45 minutes and are steeped in Scripture. The wife-husband team takes turns preaching and both are equally gifted communicators and orators. Each service ends with a reading of the Union City liturgy. (It's the liturgy- how Biblical and bridge-building- that first convinced my family to make Union City our home.)

2) Atmosphere: Union City Church is intentional about creating a welcoming space. Greeters with "welcome" signs say hi to you as you walk in and the lobby is set up with places to sit and connect with people, coffee/water/juice, and the "Connect" area for people who want to go deeper in the church. When my family and I were visiting churches, Union City was the most genuinely friendly.

2) Location: After renting space at two different locations, they have their own building just up from The White House along 16th Street NW. Built at the end of the 19th century, the building is stunning inside and out.

If you're a Christian and want a church family, consider going to Union City Church. It's led by the most thoughtful and integritous people, filled by kind congregants, and is intentional about serving the city and world.

Union City isn’t just a Church - it’s community - it’s family - it’s unity - it’s a vibe. I moved to DC from Tampa 2 years ago, and the one thing that I have been missing the most is a Church and Community that felt like what I left behind. I’ve been searching for a Church home ever since. Finding Union City has given me back something I’ve been missing - and I finally feel like I am home again.

This is a new church that’s just getting started in DC, but based on their heart for this City, the atmosphere of the gatherings, and the kindness, knowledge and professionalism of the Pastors and their launch team - you’d never know they’ve only been here for a few months.

The Church itself will launch in September but to prepare they have already started hosting small group Bible studies, worship nights, community socials, serve days, and more. The messaging from the Pastors at the pre-launch events is relevant, relatable and real.  The vibe is always positive, easy, zero pressure, judgement free and incredibly welcoming.

There is something at Union City for everyone - no matter what season of life you are in, or where you are in your walk with faith. I have already met some of the most amazing friends here, who I know will be lifelong. I am so grateful for Pastor Brandon, Pastor Delaney, and this amazing community. I cannot wait to watch this Church grow in the DMV!
Union city is a great church they make you feel so welcomed and it’s a great community of people. Will definitely make this a regular place of worship!

Union City Church is a great christian non-denominational church that God is using to make a positive impact on D.C. and the world. The preaching is exceptional, the music is impactful, the people are welcoming, and the kids program is enriching. Whether you are new to the area,  visiting for a short time, or a life long D.C. resident, we highly recommend checking out Union City Church for yourself.

A wonderful place to experience the gathered people of God in this local expression in DC. The Gospel and the Word are central to everything. Family is real and diverse. Children are encouraged to discover who God is as revealed in his word through simple and helpful catechism. The elders are humble demonstrations of what a pastor of a local church can look like. Perhaps surprisingly, this church has been an immense encouragement to our small church in Darwin, NT, Australia. Please check them out if you are on the hill!

As a member of the Church of Christ, my local church feels like home—my kind of people, my inheritance in Christ.

Everyone is friendly, and I’m part of that warm, welcoming atmosphere that embraces anyone who walks through the doors, inviting them into the life of the church. Does that sound like I'm bragging about myself?

It’s a wonderful place where you’ll hear the Truth spoken and beautifully taught, and you’ll love the singing. We don’t have a “Christian Eddie Vedder” performing solo guitar or vocal sets in front of everyone—nope! Here, the praise is acapella and accompanied by piano, and it’s lovely. Interestingly enough, one of our associate pastors, Christian Lawrence, reminds me of a member of the Hanson band. He’s a dear friend, though he doesn’t have anymore that golden mane of hair to toss aside when he’s about to pray or read the Scriptures—kind of like Moses' mantle. Despite that, everything about the church we call CHBC is great—perhaps even better than the golden hair of Michael Lawrence, whom I’ve nicknamed ‘Brother Paul Pitt’ because he’s a mix of them both!

You should come and experience it for yourself.

PS. I hope you appreciate the humor.

PS2. Michael Lawrence is single, that I know, and a godly young man.

Sermon reminded me of this Spurgeon quote which I will leave with and it says “I have a great need for Christ: I have a great Christ for my need.”
An incredible, Bible believing, God fearing congregation. A very healthy church. I have learned so much from their teachings. I wish all churches were like this!

reviews.text: While at the Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, I stopped at the museum—about a 5-minute walk away. The museum is interesting and well-designed. Someone had a good vision for it. You can see photos and props from various periods of Karol Wojtyła's life and learn facts about his life. For me, it was a special visit because I'm an emigrant, and it's nice to see that he's loved not only in his homeland. I really recommend it; it's worth spending an hour or two.

A wonderful shrine to St Pope John Paul II. Full history of his life, photos, videos, relics, and artifacts. We decided to go to view the Shroud of Turin visiting exhibit and 'The Sign' sculpture' .  We ended up spending hours there as it was a fascinating and enriching experience. The staff were friendly and happy to answer any questions.  On a practical note, the shrine has a decent sized parking lot with plenty of free parking.

We were blown away by the quality of the JP2 museum-style exhibit of the saints life and papacy. It is in the bottom floor of the building and starts with a short film… from there you wind through the exhibits detailing his life and work.  Bonus for us that there was a smaller exhibit on the life of Mother Theresa situated next to the small cafeteria area. It also was well done although just panels to read ( no artifacts). There is also a lovely small chapel with relics and a larger church contained within the building. Go see this you won’t be disappointed!!

Such a peaceful place!!!

This facility is a great way to get to know a little more about Saint John Paul II.  The exhibit is well organized and you can easily spend an hour or two here watching the video content and viewing the relics.

The gift shop was a little small and I wish there were more “merch” for the saint, but probably that is NOT the vibe they were going for.

This was such a great add to our DC trip.  The employees were beyond kind and very knowledgeable.   My group left with such a full heart and feeling very inspired.   The story of St. JP2 compliments a tour at the Holocaust Museum.  We had kids in our group and it kept their attention, too.

There is a cute little gift shop inside with lots of Catholic gifts.   There was a very comfortable area with free tea and coffee.  There were also options for purchasing snacks or a quick lunch.  We were able to eat our packed lunches in that area.   It was great.   I highly recommend making a stop here.  You won't regret it.

What a disappointing and trashy experience. I was visiting the area from AL and thought I’d visit. I don’t usually do in-person so I decided to take a risk because of the pastor’s profound messages I’ve heard on social media.
Finding the parking was a chore. I kept trying to get someone’s attention. Well apparently he (pictured)was a parking attendant; however, he was too busy shucking & jiving to serve.
I eventually found the parking garage that truly requires several turns. Walked back to the sanctuary. The same parking attendant who had ignored me told another driver to just park in the front of the church and made a space for her. reviews.text: I visited Historic Asbury United Methodist Church with a bus tour group in honor of Mary McLeod Bethune's 143rd birthday. Mary McLeod Bethune was a church member of Asbury United Methodist Church. We were greeted by the Asbury Church Historian, James A. Wright.

A historical legacy•Great leadership•
Community and civic involvement
186 Years of Black American 🇺🇸 Progress
I attended Easter 10:45 a.m. Many of my favorite Easter Hymns were sung. The sermon was divine. The choir sang beautifully and the organist played masterfully. I enjoyed the entire service.
Oldest African American church in the same location in the District of Columbia. Founded in 1836. The building was torn down in and replaced in 1915, but it is still the same church.

Every 4th Sunday, Asbury sponsors the Neighbor-to-Neighbor program where they feed 250-350 homeless residents of Washington, DC.

The brothers of Alpha Phi Alpha Fraternity, Inc.- ΟΛΑ chapter and other volunteers began aiding in this effort since September 2017.

reviews.text: My husband and I have been attending the church for about a year and a half and are so glad to have found a community away from home. The pastors are kind and give clear messages. The lead pastors and the people who attend are marked by their kindness and genuiness! I also love Capital Life’s  heart for outreach in the city to the homeless and marginalized.

reviews.text:
Rating: ★★☆☆☆

My Honest Experience With FBCG – Deep Respect for Pastor Jenkins, But Serious Concerns About the Online Campus & Staff

I want to begin by saying this respectfully and clearly: Pastor John K. Jenkins is a wonderful pastor. I have watched him for years and visited FBCG multiple times with my family before moving to New Jersey. My concerns are not with him.

My issue is with the online campus structure and the frontline staff representing the ministry.

My husband and I were online members for nearly a year. We joined with sincere hearts, seeking spiritual covering while growing our own ministries. But after 10–11 months, we made the difficult decision to leave, and here is why:

⸻

1. The online campus lacks compassion, warmth, and genuine pastoral care.

Communication was often cold, inconsistent, or dismissive. Even when we were responded to, the tone felt administrative rather than pastoral. For people seeking spiritual support, this matters deeply.

At times, it felt like the focus was more on:
• membership numbers
• class sign-ups
• participation checkboxes

…than truly caring for people’s hearts. No one should feel overlooked or “less than” because they didn’t sign up for every class.

⸻

2. I am not the only one who experienced this.

Over the years I have heard similar stories from others. This is not an isolated incident, which suggests a cultural issue among certain staff—not Pastor Jenkins.

⸻

3. This behavior is not new. I experienced something similar years ago in person.

About 7–8 years ago, my family and I went to FBCG for membership classes. We were told to come even though we were running a few minutes late after getting lost.

When my sister and I walked in, the man leading the class immediately spoke to us harshly and tried to embarrass us publicly. He had no idea my parents were right behind us. My mother confronted the behavior and said, “This is not of God. There is a respectful way to address people.” She was absolutely right.

Seeing similar coldness and dismissiveness years later online made me realize this wasn’t just one bad moment. It reflects deeper issues in how some staff members interact with people.

⸻

4. I truly hope Pastor Jenkins becomes aware of how some staff treat members.

This is said with honor. Pastor Jenkins is an exceptional leader, but I pray he knows that some staff:
• lack warmth
• lack compassion
• communicate rudely or dismissively
• fail to follow up
• treat people like numbers instead of souls

Many people join FBCG seeking healing, covering, and support. They deserve to be met with care and kindness.

⸻

5. After almost a year, we decided it was time to move on.

We were patient, prayerful, and hopeful for change. But the culture of the online campus made it clear that this simply was not the right spiritual covering for our family.

We wish FBCG nothing but blessings. We still have deep respect for Pastor Jenkins and believe in the overall mission. But I also believe ministries must prioritize:
• compassion over convenience
• people over programs
• sincerity over statistics
• true ministry over membership quotas

Sometimes it’s time to get back to the roots.

⸻

Where we stand now

My husband and I are both ordained ministers with active ministries of our own. While we haven’t opened a church yet, we were looking for spiritual covering during this season. FBCG’s online campus was not that covering for us.

This experience has pushed us to pray about:
• finding a local church home in New Jersey, or
• stepping boldly into what God is calling us to build

Either way, we trust God will guide our steps.

I’m sharing this not to tear anyone down, but because transparency matters. People entrust ministries with their spiritual lives. They deserve honesty.

I pray FBCG strengthens its communication, compassion, accountability, and care so future families don’t experience what we did. 💯🙏🏽

— Minister Ashleigh Hope Rivera
Heiress Of Hope LLC

Reid Temple is truly the best church! If you're looking for a church home that is warm, welcoming, and filled with the spirit of the Lord, look no further. The atmosphere here is inviting, and the energy is uplifting. Whether you're a first-time visitor or a long-time member, you'll feel right at home. I highly recommend stopping by – you won't be disappointed!

I want to start by saying that Reid Temple AME played a significant role in a very personal chapter of my life. I came to the church not because I was raised in religion—I wasn’t. I didn’t grow up in the church, and I wasn’t brought up through traditional Christian practices. But something drew me in.

When I chose to get baptized at Reid Temple, it was about more than ceremony—it was about cleansing. It was about releasing hurt, pain, and confusion I had absorbed from people I thought were walking with me. That moment allowed me to reclaim myself and reconnect with the Creator within me.

I realize now that my connection to God, to Jesus (in all forms and representations), and to spirit doesn’t have to come from being in a church building. It comes from the journey I’m walking as a creative, empathetic, and spiritually-sensitive individual.

Reid Temple helped me discover that. Not necessarily through the sermons or systems, but through the emotional energy exchanged, the people I encountered, and the community that formed online.

However, I’ve also realized I no longer desire to be part of any church institution. This isn’t a rejection of faith, but a redirection of it. My spiritual journey is personal, unconventional, and deeply rooted in creativity, emotion, and authenticity.

To anyone looking for a place to start their spiritual healing or self-reflection, Reid Temple may offer that spark. Just know that every journey is different. For me, it was a place that opened the door—but not the destination.

I walk with God now, freely.
And for that moment of awakening, I say thank you, Reid Temple AME.

The United Church is utterly unique, it is a blend of The United Methodist Church and the United Church of Christ, and has services in German twice a month. English language services are every Sunday at 11 AM and German language services on the first and third Sundays of the month at 9:30 AM. At 12:10 PM on Wednesdays there is a mid-week meditation.

The church has the best acoustics of any church I have ever attended, which sets off the pipe organ perfectly. There is a strong music program and members can look forward to hearing Bach, Handel, Schubert, et al.

The Church is a Reconciling Methodist Church and an Open and Affirming UCC church, which means that gays, lesbians, transexuals, and bisexuals are welcome.

The United Church prides itself on its outreach to the community with a twice monthly food pantry, On Thursday evenings at 7 PM there is Spirit Space where young adults can gather to discuss spiritual issues.

reviews.text:
The Tewhaedo Orthodox Church is a glimpse into ancient Christianity. In the Holy Liturgy, hymns, prayers, and Church leadership (i.e. priests, deacons, etc.) we show how Christianity was practiced in the first century. We believe our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is the only begotten Son of God, coequal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. We also believe we become Children of God through Holy Baptism which is often performed in this Church. In the Church’s prayers we plead for God’s peace and mercy on the sick, prisoners, poor, all members of the congregation, and the world.  The services are conducted in G’eez, which is now considered a dead language. However, there are English translations provided during service. Everyone dresses modestly and in white, for one, to mimic the angels in heaven who worship God day and night (Isaiah 6:3; Revelations 19:14; etc.)  We take off our shoes upon entering the Church because we are stepping onto Holy Ground (Exodus 3:5).  We worship from the early morning (Mark 1:35; 16:2) and at the time of Christ’s cruxifixction we partake in His body and blood through Holy Communion every Sunday.  You can feel the presence of God through the peace and love that is in the atmosphere and in our heart as we sing God’s praises. It is truly the dwelling place of God (Psalms 26:8).  This love and peace carries you through the week and your life as you navigate the struggles of life. This description is only the tip of the iceberg, there is so much more to learn, explore, in the Tewhaedo Orthodox faith. For more resources visit English.eritreantewahdo.org

Right now, the Church is praying for the health and safety of the world. At this time we are participating in Holy Liturgy through YouTube livestream Sundays starting at 6am. YouTube channel: Kidst Silase Eritrean Church DC Area. Service is led by Aba (Father) Gebresilassie.

reviews.text:
I’m truly blessed to be part of this beautiful and welcoming church community. From the moment you arrive, you can feel the spiritual atmosphere and the deep sense of tradition rooted in the Ethiopian Orthodox faith. The church services are powerful, filled with prayer, worship, and teachings that truly touch the heart.

One of the many great things about this church is the plenty of parking space available, making it very convenient for families and visitors. Whether you’re attending a Sunday service, a feast day celebration, or a weekday prayer, you’ll never have to worry about finding a place to park.

The church also offers a wonderful Sunday School program for the youth, helping the next generation grow in their faith and learn about the rich history and teachings of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. It’s a blessing to see the youth engaged and actively participating in their spiritual journey.

This church is more than a place of worship — it’s a community that supports and uplifts one another. I highly recommend visiting if you’re looking for a place to grow in your faith and connect with others in a meaningful way.

We have been coming to this church since it moved to its current location, and the development and quality of work here are truly unmatched. Parking is convenient, and the kind-hearted volunteers always make us feel welcome.

The environment brings back beautiful memories of church back home—especially during the spring and summer, when being outdoors under the trees feels so familiar. Celebrating Ledeta, Hamle Gebriel, and Good Friday (Segdet) here has been especially meaningful.Its also a plus to celebrate the special events on the day of rather than waiting until Sunday

Our family truly enjoys coming to this church, and we are very excited to be part of the journey of building a bigger church and raising our children here. May God continue to bless all the services and everyone who serves here.

I truly love attending this church. The parking is always well organized, and it’s easy to find a spot even on busy Sundays. The children’s ministry is amazing — the kids not only enjoy their time but also learn deep spiritual lessons in a fun and meaningful way.

The worship is powerful and uplifting, helping you feel connected to God and the community. The priest deliver inspiring messages that touch both the heart and the mind. Everyone is welcoming, kind, and genuine.

Overall, it’s a great place to grow spiritually, meet wonderful people, and feel part of a loving family in faith.

reviews.text:
I’ve attended Fellowship in Dallas a few times before and always appreciated the worship and warm welcome, but today’s experience was disappointing.

I brought a new friend hoping for a great service, but the sermon focused almost entirely on money and financial goals. It felt unbalanced and very off-putting. We left about 25 minutes in, while the pastor was still focused on the topic.

Today’s service felt like a financial pitch and not a message from God. I’m concerned about how a first-time visitor might perceive faith from this message.

I’ve been attending Fellowship and even served at the Grapevine campus. Currently, I attend services at the Dallas campus. My experience at Grapevine was challenging it led me to take a break because I didn’t want to accept that a church environment could feel like that. At the time, I made excuses for the people, but ultimately, the people are the church.

Since then, I’ve moved and began attending the Dallas campus. Unfortunately, I’ve experienced the same kind of disheartening interactions there. One moment that stands out happened on Mother’s Day. I shared part of my story with a young lady, I won’t mention her name, but she wore blue and had dark hair. I won’t go into detail, but I’ll say this: I’d rather have someone see or hear me suffering and do something, than witness it and remain silent.

To me, if I’m going to be a sheep in a flock, I want to be under a shepherd who weeps with his people, prays for them, reads and lives the Word, and is willing to fight the enemy on their behalf. I don’t want to be led by someone who watches people struggle and does nothing; someone more concerned with preaching a sermon than caring for the hearts of the people they serve.

From these experiences, I’ve realized where my disconnect lies with both campuses. I’ve given Fellowship chance after chance, but it’s time for me to move on.

I was trying to find a Christian church closer than Watermark Church to where I live and gave Fellowship Church a try. I've been attending Christian churches most of my life and Fellowship was absolutely one of the worst.

First of all, it's rare these days for a bucket to be passed around to make us feel awkward and guilty for not putting money into. But that wasn't the last time they begged for money, I'll get back to that later.

Secondly, after the intro words etc, I was expecting a pastor to go up to the podium but instead a movie screen popped up and we proceeded to watch a pastor speaking from another location. Huh? If I wanted to watch a pastor on a screen I'd just stay home and watch a pastor on YouTube.

Finally, this head pastor guy proceeded to basically beg for money for some new expansion that they're planning. They even handed out some super nice and expensive looking large trifold brochures about it. Those completely unnecessary and a waste of our Lord's money. He rambled on about this money put for an extended period of time. And at one point made a statement that almost made me fall out of my seat. He stated and I quote, "Oh we HAVE the money for this project... And it's in your wallet!" How bold and disgusting can one statement be?

I left that place feeling sick to my stomach knowing that my fellow Christians have obviously been led away from the priorities of our Lord. It's also sad to think that some curious non-believers will attend that excuse of a church, witness their circus and think that that's what we're all about and they will never attend another church again. I'll pray that doesn't happen. In the meantime, avoid this church until they get new leadership. God bless.

Being new to Dallas, my fiancée and I were looking for a new church home and found this one. Never have we attended a church service where the message was filled with so much hate. It was given in an aggressive and disrespectful way and was not said with love like a how a church should. We were looking for a church home where we could continue to grow in our faith and from this service, we did not find it.

Ms. Brenda is always so sweet, and the visiting pastor from North Carolina is incredibly powerful — I truly love hearing him preach.

However, during today’s (Nov 2nd) online watch service with Pastor Conway, I felt a bit thrown off. In previous sermons, he’s mentioned that he doesn’t ask for money because God provides and that the community is debt-free. But today, he shared that the McKinney church received $8 million dollars, the way it was presented felt like a push for others to give as well. Considering how many federal employees have been laid off and SNAP benefits suspended, it came across as a little insensitive. I personally only had $8 in my bank account, and hearing that message in this moment was discouraging.

A few weeks prior when I reached out in the chat for prayer and connected with Sylvia, I understand everyone has off days, but I felt a bit dismissed when I truly just needed prayer. I know no church is perfect — and I’m not expecting that — but lately, it’s been giving more of a mega-church prosperity feel, focused on money rather than ministry.
That said, I still love God, and I’ll continue to pray and stay rooted in my faith — but I won’t be watching online or visiting for now.

reviews.text: I walked in mid service right next to where the pastor was preaching. I was embarrassed but the love the congregation showed to me was unbelievable.  They didn't judge me based on appearance didn't care that I was right out of prison, in fact showed love to me even more. I found my church home.

PRAYING FOR GROWTH; GREAT PLACE TO WORSHIP

I have been attending City Church International since April and I can honestly say that I appreciate much about this church. The unity of having one location and most of the congregation attending one service carries real weight for me. Scripture tells us, “so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another” (Romans 12:5). Gathering together as one church reflects that truth in a simple and meaningful way.

The worship has been consistently excellent, not only in sound but in substance. I value that they place Scripture references under many of the songs. It reminds me of Colossians 3:16 which says, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.” They also read full passages of Scripture in their services, which should be normal but is rarely practiced by other churches. Hearing the whole counsel of God read aloud brings to mind 1 Timothy 4:13 which says, “Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching.”

I also appreciate what this church does not do. There is no merch, no sales, no pressure giving, and no marketing of personality. It feels refreshingly free of the commercial mindset that has become far too common with American churches. The communal atmosphere between services is warm, and that reflects Acts 2:42 which says, “And they devoted themselves to the apostles teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.”

There are a few areas where I would love to see growth. It is sometimes difficult to discern who the primary teacher or shepherd is. Since April, Brad has preached infrequently, and consistent pastoral direction helps a congregation in the long run. Scripture highlights the importance of clear shepherding. I Peter 5:2 says, “Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you.”

I also wish there was a more robust avenue for men to study Scripture deeply, ask questions, and be equipped to defend the faith. I Peter 3:15 commands, “but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you.” A structured apologetics or theology study would help the church obey this calling in a practical way.

Still, I have nothing negative to say about the culture or the motives of this church. Compared to many places I have attended, City Church International feels sincere, reverent, and free from self promotion. They keep the service simple and centered on Scripture, and for that I am grateful. I would gladly encourage others to visit and see for themselves.

Overall, I am thankful for my time here and pray that God continues to strengthen this church in truth, clarity, and discipleship.

reviews.text:
After attending a large church in Dallas for two years, I found myself longing for deeper fellowship, authentic community, and preaching that was both honest and rooted in Scripture. God led me to Lake Highlands Baptist Church, and it has exceeded all my desires and expectations.

From the moment I walked through the doors, I was greeted with warm smiles and genuine kindness from people who truly desired to know me. Visiting a new church can often feel awkward or intimidating, but the members of LHBC made me feel right at home.

Now, nearly a year later as a member, I can honestly say I’ve never been part of a more hospitable and Christ-centered church. The community is rich and encouraging, and each Sunday’s gathering—through the preaching of the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, and worship—consistently brings glory to God and refreshes His people.

Whether you’re searching for a new church home or attending church for the first time, you’ll find something truly special at LHBC.

LHBC has been a blessing to my Fiancé and I . If you’re new to the Dallas area, or are looking for a great church community LHBC is great. People from all walks of life attend, both young and old (well seasoned). While LHBC is strong in the area of hospitality, what made me decide to continue to come was the messages that were preached. The pastors here don’t sugar coat the Word.

Come experience God's love in a liturgically worshipful and family friendly atmosphere! A spiritual light that illumines East Dallas and surrounding areas, LHBC is a church where Jesus Christ is glorified, his Gospel is shared, his grace abounds, and his Resurrection is celebrated; where the ordinary means of grace nourish and sustain us; where God’s Word is cherished, preached, prayed, read, taught, discussed, and shared; where sin is confessed and forgiveness found; where children are welcomed, loved, and nurtured, and families supported; where every believer is encouraged to grow in Christian faith and love, and where any unbelievers are compellingly invited into freedom from sin, death, and the devil through repentance and faith in Christ.

Lake Highlands is what has truly made Dallas feel like home! My husband and I have been members of LHBC for 2 1/2 years. LHBC won our hearts by focusing on the ordinary means of grace (Scripture, Prayer, Fellowship) and by being a hospitable congregation. We have felt so loved and know at LHBC. The Lord has used LHBC to grow my understanding of the word by blessing this church with so many amazing Teachers/Preachers.

People here are very friendly but not "in your face" friendly. I didn't feel intimidated by members mobbing me before or after the service about becoming a member. They provide free coffee before and after the service, on the second floor, and you can take it into the sanctuary during the service. Or bring your own from home or Starbucks! People are generally dressed in "church casual," and everyone seems comfortable here. You come into the building on the first floor, but the entrance to the sanctuary is on the second floor. I’ve visited Shoreline City Church and, honestly, it feels like a fairly typical mega church—slick production, upbeat messages, and a big online presence. What really concerned me, though, was how they handle any honest questions about tithing. I recently left a respectful, Bible-based comment on their YouTube channel about the way they teach “you’re robbing God” if you don’t give 10% to the church budget. That comment was deleted. When I looked through their videos (with around 440k followers), almost every video has very few comments and they’re nearly all positive, which makes it look like negative or challenging comments are being filtered out.

My concern is not about giving—Christians should give. My concern is about how it’s taught. In the Bible, the tithe in the Old Testament was part of Israel’s law and mainly agricultural, used to support the Levites and care for foreigners, orphans, and widows (e.g., Deuteronomy 14:22–29). Malachi 3 was written to Israel under that covenant, not to modern churches with big building budgets. In Christ, we’re no longer under that system in the same way (Romans 6:14; Galatians 3:23–25). The New Testament emphasis is on Spirit-led, generous, cheerful giving—“not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). That means giving is ultimately between the believer and God, not something driven by fear, guilt, or manipulation.

The early church’s giving heavily prioritized people in need—widows, orphans, and struggling believers (Acts 2:44–45; James 1:27). So when a church teaches that you’re “stealing from God” if you don’t give 10% to their organization, while most of that money seems aimed at buildings, production, and comfort rather than the poor and vulnerable, I think it’s fair—and biblical—to question that. I’d feel much better about Shoreline City if they allowed open, scripturally grounded discussion on this instead of deleting comments that raise these concerns.

Update: I left

For more than two years, I was an active member and volunteer at Shoreline City Church in Dallas. I served faithfully every week, led on the usher team, and was baptized there in April 2024. When my nieces and nephew came into my care, the church even offered financial help, and I truly believed I had found a home built on love and inclusion.

Recently, after announcing my engagement to my fiancé, I was asked to step down from serving. The reasoning was made very clear; it was because of my sexuality. Hearing “thank you for your service” after years of dedication was painful, especially knowing that my life and relationship had always been known and accepted until that moment.

Not long after that meeting, on November 2, the lead pastor preached a message titled “Let Me Be Clear.” Listening to it, I couldn’t help but feel that it was directed at me and my situation. Maybe it was coincidence, but the timing and the focus of the sermon felt very personal. It was also the first time I ever heard him openly address same-sex relationships from the pulpit. His message was heard loud and clear.

In my view, the sermon finally revealed how the church truly feels about people like me. While I can respect a church’s beliefs, those beliefs should be made clear from the very beginning. People deserve honesty upfront so they can decide if that community aligns with their faith journey. Making someone feel loved, accepted, and valued for years only to later withdraw that love is deeply hurtful and misleading.

In my experience, this church focuses heavily on image, numbers, and presentation. It often felt like appearances and social perception mattered more than authenticity or transparency. During one singles event, mainstream music like Cardi B and Nicki Minaj played throughout the night, but when the event appeared online, the background music was replaced with worship songs. That was one of many moments that made me realize how much of what’s presented publicly feels curated to maintain a certain look.

I also noticed that influence and appearance seemed to play a large role within the culture. There were “reserved” seats for people viewed as having a strong image or following, and at times, it felt like how you looked or who you knew determined where you stood. While I once admired the energy and creativity of this church, over time, it began to feel more like a brand than a community.

What hurts most is knowing that there are children and teens growing up in this church, kids who might one day discover they’re different, and who currently feel loved and safe. I fear for the moment they realize that love may come with conditions. My heart also goes out to those in the LGBTQ+ community who attend and feel valued now, unaware that the same acceptance could be taken away if they ever become too visible or honest about who they are.

My intention in writing this isn’t to attack anyone but to create awareness. I want others to understand that while this church may make you feel welcomed and loved, that acceptance can change once you no longer fit their idea of what’s acceptable.

To the pastor, if by chance this message ever reaches you, my simple response to your sermon is, “It’s about time.” It’s about time the truth was spoken clearly so people can decide for themselves whether this is truly a home for them.

I’m grateful for the friendships I built here and the positive memories along the way, but I can no longer view this as a place that practices the unconditional love it preaches. I hope this review encourages others to seek a church that values people for who they truly are, not for how well they fit in their painted picture.

As someone who fell out of faith in my youth and have recently returned.  This is a great place to be accepted while learning to become closer to God.  I have plenty of good things to say about Shoreline, but what prompted this review was reading some of the negative reviews.  Some of the critiques are preferences, some are out of the control of Shoreline, and some are flat out lies.  I will address each of the following below:

Preferences:

I have seen several reviews talking about the staff not living perfect lives, particularly the pastor.  Pastor Earl openly speaks of his struggles and imperfections.  As none of us our Jesus, none of us live perfect lives to include our pastor.  If having a pastor that hides his struggle and sin is for you, then this is not a church for you.

The popularity and reach of Pastor Earl and his wife has been touched on in several negative reviews.  They use technology to reach many people and have side projects to include a podcast in which they spread the word of Jesus.  I am younger and can understand how older members may see this as an attempt to become a celebrity.  I understand differing opinions, but I have found value in the platforms with which Shoreline offers (the vast majority of which are free) to worship the lord.  On this same point, people have interpreted their actions as self promotion in an attempt to enrich themselves.  Although they ask for donations, like every church I have ever been to, I have never heard of or felt pressured during service to support any of the activities the Pastor does outside of the church to support himself and his family.  The only activity I can remember hearing about is the Pastor and his Wife's free podcast.

Out of control:

For this category, there is really only one thing talked about, but it is an extremely prominent one.  People complain about traffic and parking.  The traffic off the property of the church is very difficult to improve in my opinion.  Shoreline does not control the public roadways.  There are, however, law enforcement that assist creating a safe and efficient entrance to the property.  When it comes to parking, it may not be the most convenient, but they clearly have made a large effort to create efficient paths for those entering and leaving.  They have many employees directing people in and out of the parking lot.  Yes.... Traffic annoys us all.  For me, that is not enough to pull me from my faith.

Flat out lies:

There are a lot of very strange and in my opinion malicious lies.  I will touch on some more of the egregious ones.

I have seen complaints about not being able to find the auditorium because the building is a circle.  This is extremely strange to me as there are members everywhere holding signs that, if follow the path they create, will lead you directly to the most efficient entrance for you to use.  Also, the building is a circle, and the auditorium is in the middle of the building.  If you are going clockwise, it is always on your right.  If you are going counter-clockwise, it is on your left.  If you get there late and it is busy, they have overflow spaces of which my comment about the signs still apply to.  The members move as the place fills up to point people in the right direction.

I have seen people say that the congregation is not diverse.  I do not know what to say other than that is completely not true.  Wherever you sit, you will be around several different races.  Whatever you look like, you have a place at Shoreline.

There was a particular comment that I would like to call out that confused me.  It called the members of the church "mechanical, hippie, and conformist".  I don't see how those adjectives don't contradict each other.  I am there for my personal faith, and to enjoy the service, but there are a lot of different people who worship in many different ways.  Some people are animated, some people are reserved, some people are vocal.  I don't particularly concern myself with the ways others around me worship, but I have not seen anything that I could see as problematic.

reviews.text: Wilshire is a thoughtful and thought provoking community of faith that tries not confuse the will of the majority with the will of God.  Wilshire is a safe place to ask questions.  There are great Sunday School and choir options for all ages.

My family has attended WBC for a couple decades because it is small enough where we know a lot of people but big enough that we're always meeting someone new on a different faith journey. I like hearing about other people's views and find it refreshing that this church lets you think about things and consider there might be shades of gray but that God loves you through the process. Also, my adult kids have returned to this church, as shown by the church's young adults who went to State Fair last year together.

Our son's closest friends are kids he met at Wilshire but the reason why I'm excited to go church every Sunday (for the first time in my life) is because the sermons remind me of my best professors in college.  You didn't mind waking up at 8:00 AM because you were going to be challenged mentally and learn something new.  I'm proud to also say that we attend a church that welcomes everyone because everyone deserves to be loved.
Best church to go and experience! It is more traditional, but more loving and accepting of anyone who walks in the door. A real joy.

We joined Wilshire a little over a year ago because of this faith community’s commitment to inclusion of all. We love our church’s opportunities to serve in many many places both within the church and in the community. Our church is not a place of “just talk “ about loving people but a place of action where members serve such people as domestic violence survivors, hungry children, refugees,  victims of pay day lending and education and schools. And Wilshire is a place that celebrates beauty, art, music and drama. The “Wilshire Way” of doing things is unique, refreshing and open to all. It strives to reflect the love of Jesus both inside the church walls and out.

reviews.text: Such a beautiful sanctuary. Loving staff was very helpful and got everything rolling right away to transfer my membership from my former church. Looking forward to making this my new home church.

I love our pastors, our small group leaders, Friday morning men’s, discipleship ministries, mission trip opportunities and the worship music team is like a live concert every Sunday!!!
I love this church and this is the same place Julius Randle went to high school as well. Beautiful facility. Beautiful people as well! Amen! God Is Good!

We were visiting Dallas and wanted to try a negachurch. Giant churches can tend to get a bad rap. We wanted to decide for ourselves (we went to several on our journey from Canada). This one was very Spirit-led. It was so evident. Far more than we expected. We expected amazing production and professionalism but got so much more.

We were hugely blessed at this church. Treated like royalty when we told them our was our first time. We had front row seats! Pastor Graham came and spoke to us and we didn't even know he was the pastor until he preached. He preached truth unabashedly. You won't get a watered down gospel here. The message was powerful and I couldn't take notes fast enough. Great quote from pastor Jack in the photos.

Worship was quite the production but I don't mean that in a negative way. They are giving their best for God and it was beautiful. Orchestra, huge choir, incredible worship leaders.

After the service we visited the guest center where we were given free passes for lunch (available weekly), a book by Pastor Jack and free kids Bibles for our kids.

The free lunch was fantastic! So much variety. Menu posted. It allows for fellowship. There were hundreds there.

We checked out the gift shop and it was very unique. Not just your typical Christian bookstore wares. A lot of beautiful art especially. We bought an adorable animated kids Bible.

Fantastic experience here in every way. Our kids didn't attend the Sunday school as they wanted to stay with us so I can't speak to that.

I don't attend this church, but have come for DTS graduations and a concert long ago. Wonderful facility with a huge Kids Ministry section, large indoor playground, coffee shop, huge dining hall, large sanctuary, and more. At times, it feels like I'm in an airport terminal.

I've listened to the pastor's sermons on the radio before and he has strong messages and good teaching.

During the most recent graduation, there was a singer whose voice was mostly drowned out by the instruments. He had a very good voice from what I could hear, but I think the audio team needs to lower the volume on the instruments. I've read other reviews/complaints here about the sound. Other than that, I had a great experience.

reviews.text: Never been much for church, this place changed that in one visit! If I am not there  during service, I am watching or listening from the app. Even on vacation I listen in, now that says something! Working on becoming an official member next.

I knew by the second visit that I was going to make this church my home.  I have made many new friends.  There are great Sunday School classes for all ages.  On Wednesday night there is service for adults and Club Rock for the kids.  What an awesome way for the family to stay plugged in during the week.  If you are a man and want to learn how to be a better man, husband, father, this is the place to get connected to.  For the women and girls there is Girl Talk every few months to learn how the be a Woman of God so you can be a better girl, woman, wife, mother.  I recommend this church to everyone. name: Dallas West Church of Christ

reviews.text:
I recently found myself in a tough situation. I had run out of gas and realized I had left my wallet at home. In that moment of need, I reached out to Dallas West Church of Christ, hoping someone might be able to assist. Without hesitation, Brother Berry answered the call with grace and understanding. Although he was preparing to head into a meeting, he assured me he’d help and he kept his word. Shortly after, he and Brother James showed up, ready to assist someone they had never even met.

Their act of kindness was more than just a favor it was a reminder of what it means to be the hands and feet of Christ. They didn’t question me, judge me, or delay. They simply served and that speaks volumes.

As someone who dedicates his life to youth advocacy, mentorship, and encouraging people through platforms like my podcast (The Inspire Before We Expire) and my mental health initiative (Mental Health Matters), it was powerful to receive such genuine care and support from a church community. In a world where compassion sometimes feels rare, Dallas West Church of Christ reminded me that faith and action can still walk hand in hand.

This is more than a church it’s a family that lives the Word, supports the community, and uplifts people through love and service. If you’re looking for a place rooted in faith, integrity, and authentic care, this is it.

With deep gratitude,
Terrell Sumpter

reviews.text:
My grandbaby was baptized on Sunday.  This church is very organized and staff very friendly and accommodating.  I love how they used testimonies intertwined into the baptismal service.

My daughter enjoyed how contemporary the service was and asked me to come back to hear the Pastor preach.

We had to leave right as he was getting ready to preach.

I was surprised they did not put up a QR code or list cash app, zelle, vendors or PayPal as a mean to collect tithes and or an offering.

Sermon was good, which is what I gave this 4 stars, however, the music was way too loud and lasted too long for my liking. I was measuring and the music was averaging 107 db. As an OSHA certified manufacturer, that is very dangerous. 3 minutes of that is detrimental to hearing, let alone 30. The church should turn down the volume of their music for the safety of their congregation.
What a fantastic campus and church. The pastors are live and in person, not on a big screen, and the congregation is amazing.

I LOVE this place so much. I was a member of Elevation Church in Charlotte, NC and I was just telling a friend that I wish we had one here in Huntsville. A week later I had a friend invite me here and I was like WOW! It’s just like Elevation but a bit more intimate. The pastor walks out to the lobby afterward and greets people. Like they used to do in the smaller churches growing up. My 6-year-old just loves it too and gets upset if I’m running late. My 1-year-old loves it too. Also, our 13-year-old enjoys the service and will even ask me if we’re going to church on Sunday. I’m so happy that I found a church home for our family.

Attended this church for 5 or so years so I can give you the pros and cons (this is based on my experiences and perception) -- and I'll tell you why I had to stop attending.

Pros:
* If you're new to worship and to the church, this is a great place to get that introduction to it.
* The people (overall) in the congregation are great.
*  They manage/are responsible for Manna House, which feeds many people in our communities.
* One of the best worship music teams in the city. For me, this is the best part of the service.
* Access to several small groups so you can be involved and make connections.
* I got baptized here and will always be thankful for that.
* Great holiday productions and conferences.

Cons (for me)
* It's a baby mega church, so there are a lot of people, and you do need to put in the effort to join a small group and meet people.

Biggest Cons (and why I can't go back)
* Some of the guest speakers over the years have said some WILD and borderline illogical/insane things during their "sermons." And the pastors did nothing to stop it/correct it/address it.
* They release a financial report annually (?) but it seems kind of. . .lacking in details. This church feels more and more like a business as the years go by -- and less about Him (God).
* Both the former pastor (Pastor Rusty) and the current pastor (Pastor Scott) -- you have to often take the things they say with a grain of salt meaning they will stray away from Jesus and scripture to add too much of their own opinions, some of which make you go. . ."Now, wait, that doesn't sound like Jesus, that sounds like Pastor Rusty or Pastor Scott just using the stage to say their own thoughts."
* Pastor Scott. . .is talented as a presence on stage, but he once said during a sermon, "I've got news for you: Jesus isn't here."
* Pastor Scott. . .also used one of his sermons to talk about how angry he was and then proceeded to say, "Trans people aren't confused, they're freaks." NOW NO MATTER what you think about trans people, our job is to lead all people to Jesus, and how you going to do that by calling any people freaks? Meanwhile, there are likely people in the audience abusing their children and/or their spouses or the elderly (12 million Americans a year are victims of sexual assault and violence; 1 in 9 little girls and 1 in 53 little boys are sexually abused), but you want to use your stage time to talk about and insult less than 1% of the American population? Come on, Pastor.
* Lastly, because this getting long, Pastor Scott came into the store where I work. I was with one of my cashier and he came through her line. He didn't make eye contact and he answered a simple question they are required to ask with a tight, strained, annoyed voice. She was polite the entire time. And this is all fine sometimes -- we all have our bad days, but then he said in a later sermon how cashiers get annoyed when they are asked to simply do their jobs and how they should get another one if they can't handle it. Wow. Come on, Pastor.

Every time I want to go back because I miss the people of the Rock, I can't. The Jesus I know and the God I know loves all people. And He expects accountability from leaders (and we are all leaders). I have a new church now. Pastor Scott overall seems like a decent guy, just want to say that and pastors are only human. Just saying the Rock isn't for me anymore, but if you're new to worship (or aren't put off by any of this), it's a decent place to start.

reviews.text:
We have lived in the area for about two years and have been looking for a new church home. After resonating with Rock Creek's core and non-essential beliefs, we decided to give it a try. The service we attended was preached by a guest pastor from Arizona, but I assume that his views align with the leaders of Rock Creek considering they asked him to come preach. Overall we thought the worship was solid, everyone seemed friendly, and we have not experienced such an energetic congregation in a long time. We were initially pretty impressed and excited.

The sermon we heard was based in Nehemiah and preached on the theme of joining in when you see God working around you, told through the lens of the rebuilding of the Wall of Jerusalem. Overall, we enjoyed the message, but the frequency at which the church's building project was mentioned was very off putting. The application of this message that could have had a much more general application of "join in with God when you see him working" with a more subtle reminder of the financial contribution needed to complete the building project, but was extremely pointed toward the money the church needs for their building project. The building project was mentioned multiple times through the message and heavily focused on at the end. At one point the preacher said that if the money is not raised, they may not be able to pay staff. We were honestly shocked that this was even said.

As someone who had not previously attended the church, I felt like we were being pushed for money over and over again. It almost felt like we weren't supposed to be there - like they weren't talking to us. Obviously I understand that some messages are catered to specific people and situations and that everything may not resonate, but as a guest and potential new member we were honestly taken aback at how Scripture was used in this sermon. We are certainly open to trying Rock Creek again and are taking time to listen to other sermons that are posted online, but we did not feel that this experience made us feel strongly about pursuing Rock Creek further.

There are numerous opportunities to meet people, like in Bible study, which I’ve been able to attend three at this time, and Joyful Gatherings, where you can share experiences, hardships, and joys with other like-minded women in your neighborhood. And finally, Re-generation has been my life altering stage. Rock Creek offers this program, along with Re-engage (marriage ministry ‘counseling’).

I’m praying for anyone who takes an opportunity to read through my poorly worded review to come and visit our church community. Pastor Brad, Pastor Greg are amazing and teach the gospel of the Lord. Their passion is unwavering and every time we’re there we feel that it’s a message spoken directly to us.
